refreshed.abstractText: Accurate nuclei detection and classification in hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) whole-slide images (WSIs) is a key task in computational pathology, particularly for quantitative analysis of the tumor microenvironment. However, this task remains highly challenging due to variations in nuclei morphology, staining procedures, scanners, organs, magnifications, and WSI artifacts. In addition, many existing pipelines rely on computationally demanding architectures and post-processing procedures, making gigapixel WSI analysis time-consuming. In this work, CellPrior-Net (CP-Net) is proposed, an efficient nuclei detection and classification pipeline that utilizes a lightweight convolutional neural network architecture and hematoxylin (H) channel as prior information to enhance nuclei-aware feature learning. Extensive benchmarking was conducted against state-of-the-art pipelines on eight public and private datasets (total:∼10.4 M nuclei) obtained from different organs, scanners, magnifications, and clinical centers. Experimental results demonstrate that CP-Net achieves comparable performance while significantly reducing inference time. Furthermore, CellQuant-Net was introduced-an end-to-end nuclei quantification pipeline-that integrates a quality assessment model to exclude regions with artifacts, followed by CP-Net cell detection and classification. The pipeline is publicly available on GitHub, and provides a potentially efficient and scalable framework for downstream computational pathology applications.

refreshed.abstractText: Contrast-enhanced abdominal computed tomography (CT) scans frequently detect renal cysts, some of which may be malignant. Early and precise localization improves patient management and enables quantitative image analysis. However, current segmentation methods often lack interpretability at both feature and pixel levels, highlighting the need for an explainable approach that can detect and correct model errors. We developed an interpretable 3D renal cyst segmentation framework and validated it on 1486 cysts from 568 patients across three centers and an open-source dataset. The framework first isolated the kidney and then segmented renal cysts, integrating segmentation quality control via uncertainty estimation. A Variational Autoencoder Generative Adversarial Network (VAE-GAN) learned latent representations of 3D patches and reconstructed inputs. Latent-space modifications, guided by segmentation model gradients, generated counterfactual explanations corresponding to varying Dice similarity coefficients (DSC). Radiomics features extracted from counterfactual images, using ground-truth masks, were analyzed for associations with segmentation performance. The framework achieved a DSC of 0.82 on two external test sets, with sensitivities of 0.95 and 0.97, respectively. DSCs for original and VAE-GAN-reconstructed images showed no significant differences. Counterfactual explanations revealed how changes in cyst appearance influenced model outputs and exposed segmentation discrepancies. Radiomics features positively and negatively correlated with DSCs were identified. Using uncertainty estimates to flag segmentations with DSC < 0.75 reduced poor segmentations from 17% to 5% when only 20% of cases were sent for manual correction. This combination of counterfactual explanations and uncertainty maps improved segmentation interpretability and can be generalized for other applications.

Objective

Pretrained foundation-model (FM) embeddings are proposed as robust alternatives to handcrafted radiomic features, yet whether they better withstand segmentation-mask variability, the perturbation that radiomics intraclass-correlation (ICC) filtering exists to address, has not been tested head-to-head. We quantified how segmentation-mask perturbation propagates into feature reproducibility and downstream malignancy discrimination for FM embeddings and Image Biomarker Standardization Initiative (IBSI)-compliant radiomics measured on a common cohort. Approach. Two 2D FM encoders (BiomedCLIP; RadImageNet ResNet50) were compared against IBSI-compliant radiomics (3D, 107 features; 2D, 102 features) on the full eligible Lung Image Database Consortium and Image Database Resource Initiative (LIDC-IDRI) cohort: 556 lung nodules (300 malignant, 256 benign from radiologist consensus ratings, not pathology) from 399 patients. Up to thirteen perturbed masks per nodule (up to four reader masks, eight synthetic, one Dice-calibrated) were generated, and ICC(2,1) was computed across the ten perturbation conditions available for every nodule. Malignancy classification used L2-regularized logistic regression with patient-grouped five-fold cross-validation and bootstrap 95% confidence intervals on every area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC). Main results. Radiomics outperformed both foundation models on discrimination (AUC 0.940 and 0.930 for radiomics-2D/3D versus 0.833 BiomedCLIP and 0.798 RadImageNet; all radiomics-versus-FM differences significant by DeLong test, p≤10^(-7)). On perturbation stability the foundation models diverged: BiomedCLIP was statistically indistinguishable from radiomics (93.8% versus 90.2-92.5% stable features) and the most stable paradigm, whereas RadImageNet was significantly less stable (75.0%). A pre-specified diameter-stratified analysis showed the radiomics advantage narrows, and partly reverses, within size-matched strata; decision-curve analysis favoured radiomics. Significance. Two-dimensional foundation-model embeddings offered no discrimination advantage over IBSI radiomics under segmentation perturbation, and greater stability did not translate into greater accuracy. Perturbation stability is therefore decoupled from task-informativeness, and comparative benchmarks should report patient-grouped, size-stratified, calibration-aware metrics, not aggregate accuracy alone. .

refreshed.abstractText: Stain normalization is a fundamental preprocessing technique in digital and computational pathology, and it is important for improving the consistency of clinical diagnosis by reducing color heterogeneity. However, existing stain normalization methods are often limited by content-stain entanglement and an ambiguously modeled content-stain relationship, resulting in unstable structural preservation, cross-center adaptation burden, and sensitivity to template selection. To address these limitations, we propose a Vector-Quantized Content-Stain Decoupling Network (VQ-CSDN) that decouples structure-defining content from stain appearance and learns a center-specific content-to-stain mapping, enabling structure-preserving, template-free stain transfer from unseen source centers without source-specific retraining. VQ-CSDN employs two independent encoders to extract content and stain features respectively and a generator for reconstruction. To better characterize cross-center content feature spaces and capture staining styles, we introduce vector quantization with a global content codebook shared across centers and center-specific stain codebooks. Moreover, a content-to-stain module directly infers stain features from the content feature and a target staining style, enabling end-to-end stain transfer without template selection. To further promote structural fidelity and enhance staining style separability, we propose center-specific gradient-driven discriminators that jointly assess center-level stain conformity and the morphological consistency of generated images. Extensive experiments on multiple public and private pathology datasets show that VQ-CSDN consistently enhances normalization quality, reflected by increased SSIM/PSNR and decreased FID, and further improves downstream benign-malignant classification performance (AUC 0.9738) over state-of-the-art methods.

refreshed.abstractText: Recurrence in oral tongue squamous cell carcinoma (TSCC) remains a prognostic challenge, which necessitates additional prognostic approaches reflecting tumor biology. Therefore, we developed an objective, observer-independent, multiparametric model incorporating features of the tumoral and stromal compartments. Digitized whole-slide images from 80 patients with TSCC were analyzed using a combination of semi-automatic and deep learning-based approaches. We extracted quantitative histomorphological features, including tumor/stroma ratio (TSR), lymphocyte/stromal cell ratio in the tumor stroma (LSCR), and the modified Polsby-Popper (MPP) score reflecting tumor disjointedness. Human trophoblast cell surface glycoprotein (Trop-2) expression was assessed by immunohistochemistry in central and invasive-front tumor regions sampled via tissue microarrays (TMA) and quantified using the H-score. A composite score (CS) was constructed by summing points from these parameters; as Trop-2 did not improve cross-validated discrimination, a final three-marker CS (TSR, LSCR, MPP) was adopted as the final model. Patients were stratified into prognostic groups and recurrence-free survival (RFS) was analyzed. While individual parameters showed only trends, the CS stratified patients into poor, intermediate and favorable prognosis groups with 5-year RFS probabilities of 64.6%, 75.3%, and 100.0%. Repeated five-fold cross-validation yielded a cross-fitted consensus concordance index of 0.587 (mean per-repetition concordance index 0.567 ± 0.039), compared with an apparent concordance index of 0.676, with no evidence of a difference from conventional prognostic factors. In exploratory multivariable Firth-penalized Cox regression adjusted for pT3-pT4a category, the favorable group showed a lower recurrence hazard than the poor group (HR 0.104, 95% CI 0.001-0.854, p = 0.0316); this non-cross-validated estimate is fragile given the small favorable group without recurrence events. This observer-independent whole-slide image approach may provide complementary prognostic information to conventional histological features but requires external validation.

Background

This study sought to construct a deep-learning pipeline using an attention mechanism and multiple-instance learning (MIL) to predict early treatment response to epidermal growth factor receptor-tyrosine kinase inhibitors (EGFR-TKIs) directly from routinely available hematoxylin-eosin (H&E) whole-slide images (WSIs) of pretreatment tissue in patients with EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD).

Methods

We retrospectively obtained clinicopathological data from 100 patients with EGFR-mutant lung adenocarcinoma. The model employed ResNet-50 for feature representation and integrated a gated-attention pooling mechanism for feature aggregation at the patient level. This weakly supervised approach did not require pixel-level manual annotations and enabled direct slide-level prediction of early treatment response.

Results

The proposed gated-attention model attained an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.891 in 5-fold cross-validation, which was numerically higher than those of mean pooling (0.837), max pooling (0.821), ABMIL (0.869), CLAM (0.874), and TransMIL (0.863); however, the difference relative to CLAM did not reach statistical significance (unadjusted P = 0.062). In ablation analyses, replacing gated attention with mean pooling resulted in the largest reduction in AUC (0.054). Patient-level nuclear morphometric profiling revealed that the early adverse response group exhibited larger nuclear areas (78.3 ± 22.1 μm² vs. 62.7 ± 18.4 μm² in the favorable response group), along with elevated nuclear-to-cytoplasmic ratios, nuclear eccentricity, and chromatin texture entropy. Chromatin texture entropy was positively correlated with the model-predicted probability of adverse response (r = 0.58, P < 0.001). Furthermore, the adverse response group displayed a higher frequency of TP53-associated alterations (62.5% vs. 38.3%), which encompassed next-generation sequencing findings and p53 immunohistochemical surrogates. In exploratory analyses, a four-variable clinical model yielded an AUC of 0.792, whereas an integrated model incorporating the multiple instance learning (MIL) risk score demonstrated an apparent AUC of 0.918 in this cohort, warranting further out-of-sample validation.

Conclusion

This study demonstrates that a lightweight and weakly supervised computational-pathology model can support the early estimation of EGFR-TKI treatment response. This pipeline uses routinely acquired H&E slides without requiring additional tissue sampling, provides biologically interpretable outputs, and may support clinical decision-making in precision oncology.

We developed a deep learning (DL) framework integrating dual inverted bottleneck blocks (Dual-IB), adaptive hierarchical feature fusion, and knowledge distillation (KD) for breast ultrasound lesion classification. Background

Although heart strain analysis is useful for diagnosing cardiac amyloidosis (CA), it remains unclear which chamber best distinguishes CA from hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (HCM). This study analyzed strain in all four cardiac chambers in patients with CA and HCM using cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR) feature-tracking.

Methods

We enrolled 30 patients with left ventricular hypertrophy (15 with CA and 15 with HCM) and 17 healthy volunteers as a reference. Participants underwent 1.5-Tesla CMR to assess volume, function, and strain parameters in both ventricles and atria. The primary analysis comprised four comparisons between CA and HCM, one representative parameter per chamber (bi-ventricular longitudinal strain and bi-atrial reservoir strain), with Bonferroni correction (P < 0.0125). Additionally, exploratory analyses of the other parameters were conducted comparing patients with CA to HCM.

Results

Left atrial (LA) and right atrial (RA) reservoir strain were lower in CA than in HCM (LA: 7.1 ± 4.1% vs. 10.3 ± 3.9%, P = 0.035; RA: 10.8 ± 6.9% vs. 22.1 ± 12.9%, P = 0.005), whereas ventricular longitudinal strain did not differ. After Bonferroni correction, only RA reservoir strain remained significant. In an exploratory receiver operating characteristic analysis, the areas under the curve for LA and RA reservoir strain were 0.73 and 0.78, respectively, and did not differ significantly.

Conclusion

Bi-atrial reservoir strain was lower in CA than in HCM, and the difference in RA reservoir strain remained significant after accounting for multiplicity. Atrial reservoir strain may provide adjunctive, contrast-free functional information to help differentiate CA from HCM.

Background

Cerebral tuberculomas and brain metastases of bronchial carcinoma are often indistinguishable on magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), leading to misdiagnosis. This study develops a contrast-enhanced MRI radiomics-based nomogram to accurately differentiate them.

Methods

A total of 482 patients (290 males, 192 females; mean age 56.08±12.96 years), including 254 with cerebral tuberculomas and 228 with brain metastases of bronchial carcinoma were enrolled from two centers. Radiomic features were extracted, standardized, and reduced via significance testing, Pearson correlation, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. A radiomic model was built, then integrated with clinical predictors into a nomogram. Performance was assessed across training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curves, calibration, and decision curve analysis (DCA).

Results

A total of 13 radiomic features were selected for model development. The radiomic model demonstrated areas under the curve (AUCs) of 0.907, 0.891 and 0.886 in training, internal validation, and independent external validation cohorts, respectively, significantly outperforming models based solely on clinical factors, which achieved AUCs of 0.781, 0.712, and 0.828 (P<0.05). The nomogram, which integrated the radiomic scores (Rad-scores), age, ring enhancement, meningeal thickening, and carcinoembryonic antigen (CEA) levels, exhibited superior performance with AUCs of 0.951, 0.937, and 0.940 across the three cohorts. DCA demonstrated that the nomogram provided greater clinical net benefits across a range of threshold probabilities, and calibration curves indicated strong consistency between predicted probabilities and actual outcomes.

Conclusions

A nomogram combining clinical factors and contrast-enhanced MRI radiomics accurately differentiates cerebral tuberculomas from brain metastases of bronchial carcinoma, offering robust decision support for individualized diagnosis and treatment.

This study investigates the feasibility of using Fluorine-18 Fluorodeoxyglucose Positron Emission Tomography Computed Tomography (<sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET/CT) to preoperatively classify HGPs in CLM and secondly investigate PET parameters as prognostic markers for overall survival (OS). HGP classification was performed on tissue sections according to 2017 international guidelines. PET features (SUV<sub>mean</sub> [standardised uptake value], SUV<sub>max</sub>, metabolic tumour volume [MTV] and first-order texture metrics) were analysed to distinguish encapsulating (eHGP) from replacement (rHGP) patterns. In pretreated patients, multivariate logistic regression including both metabolic and texture parameters identified significant associations for parameters from the fixed level threshold algorithm (VuePoint Sharp IR) with small odds ratios. Overall, PET parameters showed limited ability to discriminate between eHGP and rHGP. OS was superior with eHGP versus rHGP (log-rank p = 0.045). In chemonaïve patients, SUV-based metrics showed unadjusted exploratory associations with OS after liver surgery, varying by reconstruction/delineation and were not significant after correction for multiple testing. FDG-PET-derived parameters were not reliably associated with HGP and did not support non-invasive HGP prediction in this cohort. eHGP was associated with superior survival, underscoring the value of HGP assessment for prognostication while alternative non-invasive biomarkers remain to be identified.

Objectives

Brain metastasis (BM) frequently occurs in advanced cancer patients, and accurate identification of the primary origin is essential for personalized treatment. Conventional imaging often lacks sensitivity and specificity for BM source prediction. This study aimed to develop and validate a multiparametric MRI-based radiomics model emphasizing brain-tumor interface (BTI) features to improve noninvasive BM origin identification.

Materials and methods

The primary cohort included 429 patients (740 BMs) from two centers, non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC), small cell lung cancer (SCLC), breast cancer (BC), and gastrointestinal cancer (GIC), and an independent validation cohort of 33 patients (84 BMs) from a third center. All underwent pre-treatment 3.0 T MRI with T1-weighted contrast-enhanced (T1CE) and T2-weighted (T2W) sequences. Radiomic features were extracted from tumor core and BTI regions (2, 4, 6, 8 mm). Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression was used for feature selection, and radiomics signatures (RS) were evaluated using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis.

Results

The constructed RS-BTI4 based on the 4-mm BTI region generated the best overall performance, with area under the ROC curve (AUCs) in the training cohort were 0.855 (LC/NLC), 0.910 (SCLC/NSCLC), and 0.890 (BC/GIC); in validation cohort, 0.726, 0.856, and 0.809; and in external validation cohort, 0.739, 0.750, and 0.792, respectively. RS-BTI4 consistently outperformed models based on other BTI radial widths and the whole tumor region in identifying the primary origin of BM.

Conclusion

BTI-derived radiomic features demonstrate strong potential for noninvasive identification of BM origin, with the 4-mm BTI region showing optimal predictive performance.

Key points

Question Conventional MRI cannot reliably identify the primary origin of brain metastases, particularly when the primary tumor remains unknown at diagnosis. Findings The 4-mm brain-tumor interface model showed the most favorable overall performance, measured by area under the curve, across three binary classification tasks and validation cohorts. Critical relevance statement Integrating brain-tumor interface radiomics with multiparametric MRI may improve noninvasive estimation of BM origin and support more targeted diagnostic evaluation in clinical radiology.

refreshed.abstractText:
Background

Adenomyosis is a benign uterine condition characterised by ectopic growth of endometrial tissue within the myometrium. It is associated with dysmenorrhea, heavy menstrual bleeding and subfertility. Diagnosing adenomyosis remains challenging, due to its typically diffuse distribution. A potential distinguishing feature is abnormal uterine microcirculation, which can be visualised using contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS). In our recent pilot study on the feasibility of uterine CEUS in ten participants, CEUS showed promise for diagnosing adenomyosis. The current clinical trial aims to explore if qualitative CEUS characteristics and quantitative CEUS perfusion parameters describing the uterine microcirculation can be used to differentiate between healthy controls and participants with (moderate to severe) adenomyosis.

Methods

In this explorative prospective cross-sectional study, healthy controls and participants with adenomyosis are recruited. They undergo conventional ultrasound and two-dimensional and three-dimensional CEUS. The primary outcomes are quantitative CEUS perfusion parameters. Secondary outcomes are qualitative CEUS characteristics and the relationship between CEUS findings and findings on conventional ultrasound, magnetic resonance imaging, and histopathology.

Discussion

This is the first large study to apply extensive CEUS analysis in participants with adenomyosis and compare the results with those of a healthy control group. This study will provide insights into the microcirculation of adenomyosis, which may lay the groundwork for improving diagnostics of adenomyosis.

Background and objective

Fatty infiltration of skeletal muscle and myocardium is associated with muscle dysfunction, myocardial fibrosis, and arrhythmias. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI)-based fat quantification techniques are being increasingly applied in the skeletal muscle and myocardium, but no review has systematically compared measurements in these areas. The purpose of this review was to compare the quantification of skeletal muscle and myocardial fat in terms of technical principles, clinical applications, and research paradigms.

Methods

PubMed, Web of Science, relevant journal databases, and conference proceedings (e.g., Proceedings of the International Society for Magnetic Resonance in Medicine) were searched up to December 2025 for English-language literature with the following keywords: "MRI", "fat quantification", "Dixon", "magnetic resonance spectroscopy", "T1 mapping", "T2 mapping", "skeletal muscle", "myocardium", "epicardial adipose tissue", and "artificial intelligence". Original research, reviews, and consensus statements were included.

Key content and findings

Literature onthe Dixon method, magnetic resonance spectroscopy (MRS), mapping techniques, magnetic resonance fingerprinting (MRF), and artificial intelligence (AI) was summarized. In skeletal muscle, the Dixon method is the practical standard, demonstrating robust multicenter reproducibility and established functional correlations in muscular dystrophy, sarcopenia, and inflammatory myopathies. In the myocardium, fat quantification relies mainly on mapping techniques, especially T1 mapping and epicardial adipose tissue (EAT) quantification, as Dixon and MRS techniques are limited by cardiac motion, thin walls, and low-fat content. Myocardial mapping detects subclinical injury, and increased EAT volume is independently associated with myocardial fibrosis. These techniques aid diagnosis and risk stratification in patients with dilated cardiomyopathy, arrhythmogenic right ventricular cardiomyopathy, diabetic cardiomyopathy, and Fabry disease. AI is driving automated segmentation and prognostic prediction in both fields.

Conclusions

Skeletal muscle fat quantification is predominantly conducted with the Dixon method and is relatively mature, whereas myocardial fat quantification relies mainly on mapping techniques and lacks standardization. The multicenter validation of approaches related to skeletal muscle and related experiences in automated segmentation and AI application can inform practices in the quantification of myocardial fat. Combined cardiac-skeletal muscle assessment and integrated multiparametric imaging are promising future directions in the broader field.

Purpose

To systematically review MRI-derived radiomic and artificial intelligence models predicting outcomes in men on or eligible for active surveillance (AS) for prostate cancer, and whether reported endpoints permit quantitative synthesis.

Method

Following PRISMA 2020, we searched PubMed, Scopus, Embase, and Web of Science (2000-September 2026). Two reviewers independently screened, extracted data, and assessed risk of bias (QUADAS-2, PROBAST) and methodological quality (METRICS). Three subgroups were defined: AS selection at diagnosis, baseline detection of clinically significant cancer, and progression during follow-up. Pooling was pre-specified for subgroups with at least four independent cohorts; endpoint equivalence was assessed.

Results

Seventeen studies across 12 unique cohorts were included. Seven publications derived from two cohorts; 12 independent cohort-level estimates (n = 2703) remained after overlap resolution. Nine publications (four independent cohorts) addressed progression (AUC 0.70 to 0.95), but progression was defined in five non-equivalent ways, from any grade-group increase to composite core-count criteria, precluding quantitative synthesis. Risk of bias was high or unclear in 16 of 17 studies; the median METRICS score was 32.3 % (range 18.9-52.3 %). No study reported external validation or calibration for progression.

Conclusions

Progression endpoints were heterogeneous and several were of limited clinical relevance. A core outcome set for AS (at least ISUP grade group ≥3 and/or unequivocal radiological progression), followed by multi-centre external validation with a head-to-head comparison against the PRECISE v2 (Prostate Cancer Radiological Estimation of Change in Sequential Evaluation) score, is the priority before clinical use can be considered.

Background

The efficacy of immunotherapy among patients with non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) varies, and thus reliable predictive biomarkers of response are needed. This study aimed to develop and validate a stacking ensemble learning model based on pretreatment positron emission tomography (PET) radiomics to predict response to immunotherapy in patients with NSCLC.

Methods

In this retrospective study, 45 patients with NSCLC treated with immunotherapy were enrolled. Pretreatment Digital Imaging and Communications in Medicine-format PET images were preprocessed and normalized. Tumor volumes were segmented using three methods: manual delineation, fixed standardized uptake value (SUV) thresholding with a standardized uptake value of 2.5 (SUV2.5), and adaptive thresholding (40% of the maximum SUV). Radiomics features were extracted, followed by a multistep feature selection process involving mutual information, Spearman correlation, and least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO) regression. Predictive models constructed included a stacking ensemble model [with k-nearest neighbors (KNN), logistic regression (LR), and random forest (RF) as base learners], a clinical feature-based model, and a deep learning model. Model performance was evaluated on an independent test set according to the area under the curve (AUC), accuracy, precision, recall, and F1 score.

Results

On the test set, the stacking ensemble model achieved the highest predictive performance using features from the SUV2.5 segmentation dataset, with an AUC of 0.933 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.846-0.994]. This significantly outperformed the best single model (LR; AUC=0.896) and a deep learning model (AUC =0.925). The clinical feature-based model showed moderate predictive capability, with extreme gradient boosting (XGBoost) yielding the highest AUC of 0.877 (95% CI: 0.644-1.000).

Conclusions

The proposed PET radiomics stacking ensemble model, which leverages features from multiple segmentation strategies, demonstrated superior predictive performance for immunotherapy response in NSCLC compared to single models and other benchmarks. This approach offers an effective strategy for enhancing robustness in small-sample radiomics studies and holds promise as a noninvasive decision-support tool that can aid in personalized immunotherapy stratification.

Background

Accurate identification of residual axillary lymph node (ALN) disease after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) is essential for treatment planning and for evaluating potential surgical de-escalation. We assessed the diagnostic performance of conventional ultrasonography (US), shear-wave elastography (SWE), artificial intelligence (AI)/radiomics, and multimodal ultrasound-based models for post-NAC axillary restaging.

Methods

PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Library, and Web of Science were searched from inception through December 2025. Histopathology after axillary surgery was the reference standard, and residual axillary nodal disease (ypN+) was uniformly defined as the positive target condition. Study-level 2×2 tables were harmonized to this direction. Risk of bias and applicability were assessed with the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies-2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Bivariate random-effects models and hierarchical summary receiver operating characteristic (HSROC) curves were used for modality groups with a sufficient number of independent studies; the positive likelihood ratio (PLR) and negative likelihood ratio (NLR) were pooled with random-effects models. Potentially overlapping cohorts were examined in sensitivity analyses. The study protocol was registered in PROSPERO (International Prospective Register of Systematic Reviews; registration No. CRD420251271199).

Results

A total of 14 articles were included in the systematic review, 10 of which contributed 12 test-level datasets to the quantitative synthesis. For conventional US (six studies), the pooled sensitivity was 0.55 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.36-0.73], the pooled specificity was 0.79 (95% CI: 0.73-0.84), the area under the HSROC curve (AUC) was 0.78, and the pooled PLR and NLR were 2.47 (95% CI: 1.42-4.28) and 0.54 (95% CI: 0.30-0.95), respectively. AI/radiomics models (three studies) showed a pooled sensitivity of 0.93 (95% CI: 0.80-0.98), a specificity of 0.82 (95% CI: 0.60-0.94), and an AUC of 0.94; however, likelihood-ratio CIs were wide, and the bivariate covariance estimate reached the boundary. Evidence for SWE was limited to two potentially overlapping reports, and only one multimodal combined-model study had a complete harmonized 2×2 table. At a 40% pretest probability, a negative conventional US result reduced the posttest probability of residual nodal disease to approximately 26%.

Conclusions

Conventional US alone does not reliably exclude residual axillary nodal disease after NAC. AI/radiomics approaches show promising diagnostic performance, but the evidence for this is sparse, heterogeneous, and imprecise. The currently available data do not support definitive modality ranking or omission of axillary surgery on the basis of imaging alone, and prospective multicenter external validation is required.

Background

Microvascular invasion (MVI) is a critical risk factor for postoperative recurrence and metastasis in hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC); however, reliable noninvasive preoperative prediction remains challenging. This study aimed to investigate the value of contrast-enhanced ultrasound (CEUS) in evaluating MVI in rabbit VX2 liver tumors.

Methods

Twenty healthy New Zealand rabbits were selected and used to establish VX2 liver tumor models. After 2 weeks, all models underwent conventional ultrasonography and CEUS with SonoVue (Bracco). We plotted time-intensity curves (TICs) to derive quantitative parameters, including mean intensity of the TIC (mTIC), peak intensity (PI), arrival time (AT), rise time (RT), time to peak (TTP), flow-out time (FT), and mean transit time (mTT). Based on histological diagnosis, tumors were classified into MVI and non-MVI groups. We compared the two groups in terms of the differences between VX2 tumors and the surrounding hepatic parenchyma.

Results

(I) Histological examination confirmed that 39 VX2 liver tumor models were successfully established in rabbits, with a tumor inoculation success rate of 97.50%. Among these, MVI was identified in 21 VX2 tumors. (II) Compared to tumors in the non-MVI group, those in the MVI group exhibited a larger diameter (P=0.01). Quantitative CEUS analysis revealed that the MVI group, compared to a non-MVI group, had a higher mTIC and PI (P=0.02 and P<0.001, respectively) and a shorter AT and TTP (both P values =0.03). (III) The RT of VX2 tumors was shorter than that of the surrounding liver parenchyma in both the MVI and non-MVI groups (P=0.002 and P=0.047, respectively). In the MVI group, the AT and TTP of the tumors were shorter (P=0.049 and P<0.001, respectively) while the PI was higher compared to the adjacent parenchyma (P=0.01). (IV) Receiver operating characteristic analysis showed that the PI achieved the highest diagnostic performance, with an area under the curve of 0.79 [95% confidence interval (CI): 0.65-0.93].

Conclusions

Quantitative CEUS parameters provide crucial information for evaluating MVI in VX2 liver tumors. These findings constitute experimental evidence that supports the clinical assessment of tumor aggressiveness.

Introduction

Automated extraction of slide metadata remains a major bottleneck in digital pathology, especially in settings where barcode identifiers are missing, damaged, or inconsistent. Manual transcription of case, block, and stain information is error-prone and does not scale. Building on our previous whole-slide image (WSI)-Babel-Fish framework, we developed WSI-Babel-Shark, a more extensible pipeline for reliable metadata extraction across heterogeneous slide-label layouts.

Materials and methods

WSI-Babel-Shark integrates data matrix code decoding, region of interest (ROI)-based optical character recognition (OCR), and rule-based metadata parsing within a modular Python and Docker architecture. To handle diverse institutional label formats, the system incorporates a deep learning-based label layout classifier using a ResNet-18 backbone, fused with handcrafted descriptors and prototype-based open-set recognition to categorize labels into 10 predefined layout groups. A graphical interface supports ROI annotation, dataset management, and configuration editing. Performance was evaluated on 270 WSIs (.svs and .ndpi formats) and cross-validated using 110 slides from the previously published WSI-Babel-Fish dataset to assess backward compatibility.

Results

The label layout classifier achieved an overall accuracy of 97.4%, with macro-averaged precision, recall, and F1-score of 0.98 while reliably rejecting previously unseen layouts. End-to-end pipeline evaluation achieved complete SlideID reconstruction for 258 of 267 evaluable WSIs (96.6%). Independent comparison of OCR-derived metadata with the corresponding Data Matrix-decoded metadata on 236 slides demonstrated complete metadata concordance for 230 slides (97.5%), whereas field-level concordance ranged from 98.3% to 100.0% across all evaluated metadata fields. Cross-dataset analysis confirmed full compatibility with WSI-Babel-Fish label structures.

Conclusion

WSI-Babel-Shark advances automated metadata extraction from WSIs by introducing a label-layout classification framework validated on heterogeneous label layouts and incorporating open-set recognition, together with standardized ROI annotation and a fully containerized implementation. The framework ensures reproducible linkage between digitized slides and lab information, is designed to facilitate interoperability with lab information systems, and provides a scalable foundation for large-scale digital pathology workflows. The complete implementation is openly available at: https://github.com/cpheidelberg/WSI-Babel-Shark.

Background

Reliable mitotic identification in whole-slide images (WSIs) is essential for prognostic evaluation and tumor grading; yet, many commercial artificial intelligence (AI) pathology platforms function as opaque black boxes with little auditability and, frequently, little expert supervision throughout development.

Methods

We developed a transparent and repeatable process for mitosis identification using YOLOv8, designed to scale from full slide inference to patch-level benchmarking. Global non-maximum suppression (NMS), GPU accelerated inference, region of interest-driven and adaptive tiling, and tissue gating are all integrated into the pipeline. In order to facilitate expert validation and traceability, audit-ready outputs include detection CSVs, tile manifests, positive and negative overlays, and heatmaps.

Results

From small clinical slides (26 tiles, 4 detections) to huge benchmarks (TUPAC SP2 with 14,270 tiles, 1754 detections), six typical WSIs were processed. Whereas throughput averaged 78 tiles/s depending on the slide size and tissue dispersion, average confidence scores remained constant between 0.69 and 0.80. The successful generation of all audit outputs attested to its scalability and reproducibility.

Discussion

Transparency and expert monitoring are given priority in this pipeline, in contrast to many industry systems that place an emphasis on end-to-end automation. Whereas audit outputs enable reviewers to track each detection, explicit recording of positive detection tiles avoid quiet false positives. Evaluation on a small number of WSIs and the lack of benchmarking against annotated entire slide datasets are among the limitations, highlighting the necessity for more extensive and thorough cohort validation. Another significant drawback of this work was the use of a single GPU for inferencing.

Conclusion

This study develops a therapeutically focused, audit-ready process for mitotic figure detection, hotspot identification, and decision-support tool by fusing technical rigor, vetted by experts throughout the process. By demonstrating scalability, reproducibility, and transparency, this work is positioned as a proof-of concept for clinical mitosis detection, multi-GPU/cloud deployment, lab information systems/LIMS connectivity, and eventual use in digital pathology work processes. It also offers a trustworthy and marketable illustration of AI's potential in pathology.

refreshed.abstractText: Fresh-cut apples undergo rapid enzymatic browning, which compromises visual quality and causes substantial postharvest losses. Most RGB vision approaches rely on handcrafted color/texture descriptors that are sensitive to acquisition conditions and provide limited linkage to the underlying enzyme dynamics. This study proposes a radiomics-enhanced RGB imaging framework to non-destructively quantify browning progression and predict key browning-related enzymatic activities in fresh-cut "Red Fuji" apples. Apple slices were imaged from 0 to 24 h after cutting using a custom high-resolution RGB setup under controlled illumination. Browning regions were automatically cropped from the original photo, and high-throughput radiomic features were extracted from regions of interest with PyRadiomics, including first-order statistics, 2D shape descriptors, and multi-scale texture features from original, wavelet-transformed, and 2D local binary pattern (LBP2D) images. A variance filtering plus Elastic Net selection pipeline produced a compact set of 58 informative and weakly correlated features dominated by wavelet textures. Five regressors (KNN, SVM, EN, DT, and MLP) and four ensemble strategies (Bagging, Boosting, Voting, and Stacking) were evaluated using repeated cross-validation. The best single models achieved R<sup>2</sup> of 0.909 (Time), 0.966 (BI), 0.950 (PPO), and 0.918 (POD), while ensemble learning consistently delivered robust performance with R<sup>2</sup> generally >0.90 (e.g., voting: 0.913 for Time, 0.972 for BI, 0.924 for POD). These results suggest that radiomic features extracted from low-cost RGB images may provide a useful approach for estimating browning and selected enzyme activities in fresh-cut 'Red Fuji' apples under the conditions investigated.

Background

Percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL) is a common surgical intervention to treat renal calculi. Excessive irrigation fluid absorption during surgery may enhance extravascular lung water (EVLW) level. Hence, accurate monitoring and protocolized management of EVLW are crucial for preventing postoperative complications.

Methods

Our randomized controlled study enrolled 181 cases undergoing elective PCNL and randomly divided them to conventional CVP-based fluid management (Group C) or lung ultrasound-guided protocolized fluid management (Group LUS). Primary outcomes included increased incidence of EVLW and severity within 30 min postoperatively and postoperative hypoxemia in the two groups. Secondary outcomes were the CVP values and LUS scores at the following time points: before irrigation (T0), at the first administration of furosemide (T1), after irrigation (T2), and at the time of leaving the post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) (T3). Moreover, included fluid volumes (crystalloid, colloid, total infusion, irrigation, and supplemental fluid at first furosemide administration), total furosemide dosage. The anesthesia time, surgical duration, PACU stay time, extubation time, and total hospital stay were recorded. Safety outcomes included perioperative complication rates.

Results

Compared with Group C, Group LUS demonstrated significantly lower incidence and severity of EVLW increase within 30 min postoperatively, as well as reduced postoperative hypoxemia rate (all p < 0.001). Group LUS displayed evidently lower LUS scores and CVP values at T1、T2 and T3 than Group C (p < 0.001). Moreover, extubation time and PACU stay in Group LUS were significantly reduced, compared to Group C (p < 0.05).

Conclusions

An LUS-guided fluid management protocol integrating real-time EVLW assessment with predefined intervention thresholds outperformed conventional CVP-based management during the perioperative period of PCNL. The superior sensitivity of LUS for detecting early EVLW elevation, combined with protocolized early intervention, reduced postoperative hypoxemia incidence, shortened extubation time and PACU stay duration, and improved short-term perioperative recovery.

Background

Perineural invasion (PNI) in tongue squamous cell carcinoma (TSCC) is associated with aggressive behavior and poor outcomes, yet it can be under-recognized on H&E sections because it is often focal and interpretation varies. Manual assessment of PNI suffers from significant interobserver variability, motivating AI-based decision support. We developed and externally validated a weakly supervised WSI model to predict PNI in TSCC.

Methods

We retrospectively analyzed 1,511 digitized H&E whole-slide images from 629 patients at two centers. Patient-level partitioning yielded an internal training cohort of 305 patients and 787 WSIs, an internal validation cohort of 132 patients and 340 WSIs, and an external test cohort of 192 patients and 384 WSIs. Non-overlapping tiling generated 41,552,500 candidate patches before tissue-background exclusion, of which 7,813,555 unique tissue patches were retained for analysis. A two-stage pipeline was used: patch-level modeling and MIL-based slide aggregation. ResNet50 was selected over Inception_v3 and SimpleViT as the feature extractor. Patch-level prediction probabilities and image features were aggregated into a 101-dimensional patch likelihood histogram (PLH) and a 101-dimensional visual bag-of-words (BoW) representation, respectively. For conventional classifiers, the two representations were concatenated into a 202-dimensional vector, followed by z-score normalization and LASSO feature selection. For the Transformer, the two representations were processed separately using PCA, independently projected into 128-dimensional embedding spaces, and integrated using four-head cross-attention. Performance was assessed by ROC, decision curve analysis (DCA), and calibration.

Results

The internal training, internal validation, and external test cohorts included 305, 132, and 192 patients, respectively. PNI prevalence was 82.3%, 79.5%, and 72.9% in these cohorts, respectively. The Transformer fusion model achieved AUCs of 0.990 in the training cohort, 0.968 in the internal validation cohort, and 0.940 in the external test cohort. Calibration and decision curve analysis were used to characterize the model's predicted probabilities and modeled net benefit in the retrospective study cohorts. Patch-level Grad-CAM was used to generate qualitative saliency visualisations associated with ResNet50 patch-level PNI scores.

Conclusions

This externally validated computational pathology application demonstrated retrospective technical feasibility for WSI-level PNI prediction in TSCC and has potential clinical utility for flagging slides for focused pathologist review. Its effects on clinical workflow and postoperative decision-making require prospective evaluation.

Purpose

To develop and externally validate a peri-ablational contrast-enhanced CT radiomics model for predicting early hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) progression after microwave ablation (MWA) and to assess its incremental value over clinical predictors.

Methods

This retrospective multicenter study included 376 patients in training (n = 235), internal validation (n = 60), and external validation (n = 81) cohorts. Early progression was defined as local tumor progression or new intrahepatic HCC within 1 year after MWA. Radiomics features were extracted from 5-mm peri-ablational regions on multiphasic CT obtained 1-2 months after MWA. Six machine-learning algorithms and phase combinations were evaluated. The selected radiomics model was combined with independent clinical predictors. Discrimination, calibration, clinical utility, and model interpretability were assessed.

Results

The arterial-plus-portal venous phase (AP + PP) multilayer perceptron model achieved AUCs of 0.857, 0.815, and 0.903 in the training, internal validation, and external validation cohorts, respectively, with performance comparable to the three-phase model. Log10 AFP and tumor size > 2 cm were independent clinical predictors. The combined clinical-radiomics model achieved AUCs of 0.926, 0.884, and 0.963, respectively. In external validation, sensitivity, specificity, and accuracy were 84.2%, 96.8%, and 93.8%, respectively. SHAP analysis identified the radiomics score as the most influential predictor.

Conclusion

Peri-ablational AP + PP CT radiomics combined with AFP and tumor size demonstrated good discrimination for early HCC progression after MWA and may facilitate individualized risk assessment, pending further validation.

new_candidates.abstractText: Artificial intelligence (AI) is permeating many aspects of daily life. Medicine, and specifically orthopaedic surgery, is being influenced by the rapid growth and success of AI in serving as an adjunct to medical expertise. AI includes many nested subfields and applications such as computer vision, language models, and predictive analytics. Using standard machine learning methods, clinical decision support tools are being developed for clinicians to provide evidence-based, individualized care. Some models predict clinical and functional outcomes after a procedure, whereas others may incorporate administrative metrics to predict factors, such as length of stay, return to the emergency department, and complications. The application of AI to medical imaging focuses on the extraction of a large amount of quantitative data in the form of predefined features from clinical images that humans cannot perceive, a field known as radiomics. There has been recent interest, particularly in oncology, to apply radiomics to aid in diagnosis and prognostication of outcomes. Given the robust growth of radiomics literature, and the anticipated application in orthopaedic surgery, the purpose of this review article is to educate the orthopaedic surgery community on the practical importance and the basics of radiomics.

Opinion statement

Soft tissue sarcomas represent a diverse set of malignancies with equally diverse behavior, ranging from relatively indolent low-grade tumors to aggressive high-grade tumors with high metastatic potential. Initial diagnosis hinges on tissue biopsy for determining histologic subtype and grade, while conventional imaging plays critical roles in defining local tumor size and extent, staging, treatment response, and disease surveillance. However, conventional semantic interpretation of imaging studies overlooks much of the complex imaging data embedded in routine clinical studies. Radiomics encompasses the identification of novel disease biomarkers extracted from highly quantitative characterizations of tumor structure and heterogeneity and has shown promise in providing a deeper understanding of soft tissue sarcomas. Given the increasing usage of imaging in soft tissue sarcomas, particularly usage of MRI, it behooves both clinicians and radiologists to further the depth of understanding that may be gleaned from radiomics. These insights, although primarily experimental, represent a rapidly evolving landscape in soft tissue sarcoma diagnosis and management where radiomics will be increasingly integrated into clinical practice. The present work focuses on the latest updates with regards to the application of radiomics to the diagnosis, prediction of treatment response, assessment of treatment response, and prognosis of soft tissue sarcomas and how they may affect sarcoma management.

Objective

Accurate preoperative prediction of lymph node metastasis (LNM) in colorectal cancer remains challenging using conventional CT assessment. This proof-of-concept study compared CT-based multi-station lymph-node radiomics with primary-tumor radiomics for patient-level preoperative prediction of LNM.

Materials and methods

This single-center retrospective study included patients with pathologically confirmed colorectal cancer who underwent preoperative contrast-enhanced CT and surgical resection. Patients were divided into training and validation cohorts. Radiomics features were extracted from the primary tumor and visible regional lymph nodes across multiple nodal stations. Three radiomics strategies were developed and compared: primary-tumor radiomics, multi-station lymph-node radiomics, and combined radiomics. Model performance was assessed using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC), calibration analysis, decision curve analysis, and five-fold cross-validation. Pairwise AUCs were compared using the DeLong test. A clinical-radiomic model was further constructed by integrating the optimal radiomics strategy with preoperative clinical variables.

Results

In the validation cohort, the multi-station lymph-node radiomics model outperformed the primary-tumor radiomics model for predicting LNM (AUC, 0.864 versus 0.637; p = 0.0055). The combined radiomics model achieved an AUC of 0.840, without significant improvement over the lymph-node model (p = 0.2211). After integration with clinical variables, the clinical-radiomic model achieved an AUC of 0.879.

Conclusion

CT-based multi-station lymph-node radiomics showed significantly higher validation performance than primary-tumor radiomics for patient-level preoperative LNM prediction in colorectal cancer. However, this single-center proof-of-concept model is not ready for direct clinical implementation and requires multicenter external validation before clinical translation.

Key points

Question Can CT-based multi-station lymph-node radiomics improve preoperative nodal metastasis prediction beyond primary-tumor radiomics in patients with surgically treated colorectal cancer? Findings Multi-station lymph-node radiomics achieved higher validation performance than primary-tumor radiomics for patient-level prediction of pathological lymph-node metastasis in colorectal cancer. Relevance statement CT-based multi-station lymph-node radiomics may support individualized preoperative nodal risk stratification in colorectal cancer, but multicenter validation and prospective evaluation are required before clinical translation.

new_candidates.abstractText: Radiomic features provide a quantitative description of tissue organization in histopathology images. QuPath, a widely used open-source platform for whole-slide image analysis, offers morphology, intensity, and Haralick texture measurements but no standardized radiomic feature set such as that of PyRadiomics. Researchers must therefore export data to external Python pipelines, interrupting their QuPath workflow. QuRad extracts radiomic features from cell detections and annotation regions directly inside QuPath. The extension and equivalent Groovy script implement 119 features: 103 two-dimensional features enabled by default and 16 optional legacy shape descriptors. We compared QuRad 0.4 with PyRadiomics 3.0.1 on identical grayscale images and pixel masks. All 103 default features met a 10<sup>-9</sup> absolute-or-relative agreement tolerance on a breast-cancer benchmark tile (410 cells). On 20 melanoma tiles (8,644 nuclei), 97 of 103 features met this tolerance and 6 polygon-derived shape features differed from PyRadiomics' raster-derived mesh (minimum concordance correlation coefficient 0.942). The 22 synthetic regions accepted by PyRadiomics reproduced the expected intensity and texture values. A single-threaded server benchmark reached about 1,900 nuclei per second, and processing the 184,242 cells of a whole-slide image took 2.7 min on a laptop. A random forest distinguished tumor cells from lymphocytes in melanoma (pooled macro-F1 0.853) and classified 197 tissue regions of 6 breast-cancer slides into 3 compartments (0.696). QuRad exports the features with object coordinates and extraction settings for use in QuPath or downstream analyses.

Purpose

The aim of this retrospective monocentric study is to examine the role of radiomics in distinguishing benign and malignant adrenal incidentalomas (AIs) analyzing computed tomography (CT) images.

Material and methods

We retrospectively selected patients with clinical or histologic diagnosis of adrenal pathology studied in the period 2011-2025 with pre-operative or pre-diagnostic CT in our center. Two radiology residents and a radiologist with 10 years of experience delineated the volume of interest of the AI using 3D-slicer software. All 135 patients included in the analysis underwent segmentation of the non-contrast acquisition; among these, 115 were also segmented on the portal phase acquisition. Statistical analysis was performed by dividing patients into two groups: group 0, benign adrenal pathology (adenoma, myelolipoma, ganglioneuroma, pseudocyst); group 1, malignant adrenal pathology (pheochromocytoma, adrenal cortical carcinoma, metastasis, lymphoma).

Results

135 patients were included. On non-contrast acquisition, the logistic regression model LASSO selected three first-order features and two second-order features able to distinguish patients belonging to Group 0 or Group 1. The features selected were used to construct a radiomic model that showed excellent AUC/discrimination (AUC: 0.88-95% CI 0.83-0.94). For portal phase, the logistic regression model LASSO selected three first-order features and two second-order features able to distinguish Group 0 and Group 1. The features selected were used to construct a radiomic model that showed excellent AUC/discrimination (AUC: 0.84- 95% CI 0.77-0.91).

Conclusion

The radiomic models developed from both non-contrast and portal CT phases were effective in differentiating benign from malignant AIs.

new_candidates.abstractText: Radiomics has emerged as a transformative tool in medical imaging, offering the ability to extract complex quantitative features that are generally indiscernible to the human eye. These radiomic features can be interrogated non-invasively on medical imaging. Importantly, in contrast to traditional diagnostic methods reliant on a single, often scalar, measure, radiomics features can form a high-dimensional data space from imaging data suitable for machine learning. Within the framework of artificial intelligence, radiomic features can be harnessed for differentiating healthy from pathological tissue, risk-stratifying patients for benign and malignant fractures, and clinical outcome measures. This review presents an introduction to the methodology underlying radiomics feature selection, reproducibility, feature analysis and model building, assessment of model performance, and open-source libraries for extracting radiomics features from imaging. The review then highlights the application of radiomics in osseous and cartilaginous spinal imaging for identifying osteoporosis and the prediction of fragility vertebral fractures, chronic low back pain and the assessment of intervertebral disc degeneration and herniation, cancer metastatic spine disease and the differentiation of benign vs. malignant lesions and the classification of benign vs. malignant vertebral fractures. Throughout this stage, we endeavor to demonstrate how radiomics can analyze imaging biomarkers to detect subtle structural changes in vertebral bone microarchitecture, assess tissue quality and early-stage fractures, and identify radiomic biomarkers of low back pain chronicity and intervertebral disc heterogeneity that signal degeneration and herniation risk. The review culminates with the presentation of the current limitations and future research directions, including opportunities for integration with multi-omics analysis, highlighting radiomics' potential for enhanced diagnostic accuracy and more personalized patient care. The application of radiomics in spinal imaging offers a promising avenue for improving non-invasive image early detection, risk stratification, and personalized management of spinal pathology, paving the way for more effective interventions and improved patient outcomes.

Objectives

Salivary gland ultrasonography is a promising non-invasive modality for the evaluation of Sjögren's disease (SjD), but its diagnostic utility is limited by operator dependency. This study aimed to evaluate the classification performance of radiomics-based machine learning using parotid gland ultrasonography and to compare it with conventional visual assessment.

Methods

A total of 866 parotid gland ultrasound images from 202 participants were included: 123 patients fulfilling the 2016 ACR/EULAR criteria for SjD, 33 healthy controls, 24 non-Sjögren sicca patients, and 22 incomplete SjD cases. A total of 104 radiomic features describing intensity, texture, and micro-texture patterns were extracted. A 5-fold soft-voting SVM ensemble was trained on confirmed SjD and healthy participants; non-Sjögren sicca and incomplete SjD cases were reserved for the held-out test set. SHAP analysis was used for model interpretability.

Results

The SVM ensemble achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.99 for binary classification between SjD and healthy controls, with 0.94 accuracy, 0.86 sensitivity, and 0.96 specificity, outperforming radiologist assessments (accuracy: 0.62 and 0.72). SHAP analysis identified intensity dispersion metrics, GLCM-based texture features, and LBP micro-texture patterns as the strongest predictors. PCA and feature-level analyses demonstrated substantial overlap in radiomic features between non-Sjögren sicca and confirmed SjD patients.

Conclusion

Radiomics-based machine learning demonstrated high classification performance for distinguishing SjD from healthy controls using parotid gland ultrasonography. Quantitative ultrasound analysis may serve as an objective adjunctive tool in SjD assessment, although validation in larger multicenter cohorts is required.

new_candidates.abstractText:
Background

Pain is the hallmark of knee osteoarthritis (KOA) and a major cause of disability. Identification of individuals at high risk of pain progression may facilitate timely intervention. The infrapatellar fat pad (IPFP) has been implicated in KOA-related pain. We aimed to evaluate whether baseline and longitudinal delta MRI-derived IPFP radiomic features can predict pain progression.

Methods

This study used the Foundation for the National Institutes of Health (FNIH) Osteoarthritis Biomarker Consortium dataset from the Osteoarthritis Initiative (OAI) for model training and hold-out validation, while the Pivotal OAI MRI Analyses (POMA) dataset was used for independent validation. A total of 919 knees with baseline and 24-month MRI examinations (1838 scans) were included. We extracted the radiomic features of IPFP and developed a baseline radiomics model as well as a longitudinal delta-radiomics model over two years. Model performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUC-PRC), and compared with the clinical model and a whole-joint MRI Osteoarthritis Knee Score (MOAKS) model.

Results

The baseline IPFP radiomics model exhibited stable predictive performance, with AUC-ROC values of 0.731 and 0.732 in the hold-out and independent validation sets, outperforming clinical and MOAKS models. In the independent validation set, the model yielded an AUC-PRC of 0.257, substantially exceeding the positive event prevalence (0.115). Notably, the delta-radiomics model further improved performance, achieving AUC-ROC values of 0.861 and 0.806 in corresponding validation sets and an AUC-PRC of 0.434 in the independent validation set. More importantly, the IPFP radiomic score was confirmed as an independent predictor of KOA pain progression in multivariable regression.

Conclusion

Quantitative MRI radiomics of the IPFP provide a promising tool for predicting KOA pain progression.

new_candidates.abstractText: Imaging is increasingly essential for the diagnosis, prognostication, and management of cancer patients. It is a field in rapid evolution and has the potential to provide noninvasive characterization of malignancy, which remains an important Holy Grail of medicine. Radiomics, which involves the high-throughput assessment of imaging features, aims to transform images into structured phenotypic data. By correlating imaging-derived data with clinical and molecular information, radiomics offers the potential to relate tumor biology to imaging phenotype to improve patient prognostication and management. This review surveys the principles and applications of classical and deep learning-based radiomic approaches in oncology, and it highlights key challenges in robustness and reproducibility that must be addressed to realize the potential of radiomics in clinical practice.

Inclusion criteria focused on peer-reviewed studies in English on radiomics applications; 50 studies were ultimately evaluated after excluding non-relevant works. The purpose of this article is to systematize the utilization of radiomics in assessing thyroid nodules, aiming to furnish valuable theoretical insights. As an emerging interdisciplinary domain, radiomics integrates medical imaging with computer data analysis techniques, thus constituting a potent instrument for precise diagnosis and comprehensive evaluation of thyroid nodules. Through a scrutiny of the principles, methods, and applications of radiomics in thyroid nodule evaluation, we aim to elucidate its potential for enhancing diagnostic accuracy, assessing disease progression, and mitigating overdiagnosis.
